screens.title: What is Amazon EBS?
screens.narratorSegment: Amazon EBS is persistent block storage that you attach to EC2 instances. Unlike instance store volumes that are ephemeral and tied to an instance’s lifetime, EBS volumes persist independently, so you can stop or replace an instance without losing data. This independence enables operational tasks like detaching a volume from one instance and attaching it to another in the same Availability Zone, or creating a snapshot as a backup. A concrete example: your web server’s root volume can be an EBS volume so you can stop the instance for maintenance and restart it later with the same disk content intact. A common misconception is to treat EBS like network file storage; it behaves like a raw disk device inside the instance and must be formatted, mounted, and managed by the OS. Key operational implications are that you must keep zone alignment for attachments and consider performance characteristics — block storage presents raw input and output characteristics to the operating system, and your file system and applications determine observed latency and throughput. To check understanding, ask: when would you prefer instance store instead of EBS, and why might that be rare for production systems?

Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › What is Amazon EBS?
Amazon EBS: persistent block storage
EBS volumes behave like disks attached to an instance and persist independently of instance lifecycle.
Analogy
Think of EBS as a virtual hard drive you can detach, snapshot, and reattach to other servers in the same zone.
Misconception
It is not networked file storage. EBS is block-level and must be formatted and mounted by the OS.
Key Takeaway

EBS persists beyond the EC2 instance and acts as a disk. Manage attachments, formatting, and snapshots like physical storage.

Comparison: EBS vs Instance Store
  • EBS: persistent, attachable, snapshot-capable, zonal.
  • Instance store: ephemeral, tied to instance lifecycle, higher I/O for some instance types but not persistent.
  • Operational rule: use EBS for OS and data disks in most production cases because of persistence and snapshots.
Concrete example
A web server root on EBS lets you stop the instance for updates and restart with the same disk. You can also create a snapshot before upgrades to revert if needed.

screens.title: EBS Volume Types Overview
screens.narratorSegment: EBS provides several volume types optimized for different workloads. General Purpose SSDs (gp2 and gp3) suit a wide range of transactional workloads such as boot volumes, dev/test, and low-latency interactive apps. gp3 improves cost control by letting you provision IOPS and throughput independently of size; for example, a gp3 volume can deliver 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB per second regardless of size. Provisioned IOPS SSDs (io1 and io2, including io2 Block Express) are for input and output-intensive workloads like large relational or NoSQL databases that need sustained high IOPS and low latency; you explicitly provision IOPS and throughput. Throughput Optimized HDD (st1) is a low-cost choice for large sequential workloads such as big data or log processing where throughput matters more than random IOPS. Cold HDD (sc1) is the lowest-cost option for infrequent access or archival-like datasets. A common operational mistake is using general-purpose SSDs for sustained high-IOPS databases or using io1 for trivial boot volumes; both lead to avoidable performance or cost issues. The right selection comes from profiling your workload’s read/write patterns and balancing cost with required latency.

gp2 / gp3
Balanced, general-purpose SSDs. Use for boot volumes, dev/test, and interactive apps. gp3 separates IOPS and throughput from size for better cost control.
io1 / io2 (Block Express)
Provisioned IOPS SSDs for databases and latency-sensitive workloads. Provision required IOPS explicitly; io2 Block Express supports the highest IOPS and durability.

  • Use st1 for large sequential workloads like data warehouses or ETL pipelines.
Concrete example
For a transactional database with predictable high IOPS, choose io2 and provision the IOPS you need; for a web server boot disk, gp3 is usually sufficient.

screens.title: gp3 vs gp2: provisioning IOPS and throughput
screens.narratorSegment: gp3 is the newer general-purpose SSD generation that decouples IOPS and throughput from volume size, which gives you more control and cost-efficiency. In gp2 IOPS scale with size and burst credits can be exhausted, causing throttling. When provisioning, remember gp3 removes the need to increase storage capacity just to gain IOPS. A common misconception is thinking gp3 automatically provides higher baseline IOPS for free; you must explicitly provision additional IOPS beyond the baseline. Operationally, pick gp3 for boot volumes and many production workloads where you want predictable and independently tunable IOPS and throughput. Example create and attach commands, and OS validation steps.

lsblk

Increasing volume size to gain IOPS is unnecessary with gp3 and may waste storage cost; instead increase IOPS or throughput directly.

screens.narratorSegment: Provisioned IOPS SSDs — io1 and io2, including io2 Block Express — are designed for workloads that require sustained high IOPS and predictable low latency, typical of large relational or NoSQL databases. screens.title: EBS Snapshots: incremental backups
screens.narratorSegment: EBS snapshots are incremental backups of a volume stored in Amazon S3. When you create a snapshot, only the blocks that have changed since the previous snapshot are saved, making snapshots space- and time-efficient. To restore, you create a new volume from the snapshot; that new volume represents the state of the original at snapshot time. screens.title: Fast Snapshot Restore (FSR)
screens.narratorSegment: Fast Snapshot Restore is a capability that pre-provisions data from a snapshot into a specified Availability Zone so that volumes created from that snapshot are immediately available at full performance. EBS snapshots are incremental backups of a volume stored in Amazon S3. When you create a snapshot, only the blocks that have changed since the previous snapshot are saved, making snapshots space- and time-efficient. A concrete example: after taking a snapshot of a 100 GiB data volume, subsequent snapshots only store changed blocks, saving storage.
